hooks.text: Most bar soap starts as rendered animal fat. I'm not being rude about it — that's what soap has been for four thousand years, and there's a reason it's still the default.
There is one fat in this bar. Not one main ingredient. One.
People ask what's in the base and the answer is short enough that it makes them suspicious.
Soap is a chemical reaction, not a recipe. Once you know which reaction, the back panel of most bars stops making sense.
A customer told us our bar was a third gone after a week and eleven dollars was excessive. They were right about the week.
Eleven dollars for a bar of soap. The complaint we actually get isn't the price — it's how fast it goes. Those are two different problems and only one of them is ours.
Our bar dissolves faster than the one in your shower right now. That's not a defect, and I can tell you exactly what it's buying you.
The most common thing people get wrong about this bar costs them about six weeks of it.
If your skin reacts to things you probably won't switch from body wash to a bar. You're right to be careful — most bars earned that.
That squeaky-clean feeling you were taught to want is the sound of something being removed.
Our bar leaves a slightly grippy feel and some people hate it. I'd rather explain what that is before you order than after.
We leave something in this soap that almost every commercial soapmaker takes out — and then sells separately, because it's worth more on its own.

bodies.name: One fat
lines: Most bar soap starts as rendered animal fat — tallow — held together with synthetic detergents and something the label just calls fragrance.
That isn't a scandal. Tallow is cheap, it's stable, and it makes a hard bar that survives a wet soap dish. Every one of those is a real advantage and we gave all three up.
We use one fat. Organic virgin coconut oil, cold-pressed, unrefined, saponified — that's the reaction that turns an oil into soap.
Refined coconut oil would be cheaper and it wouldn't vary batch to batch. Unrefined keeps what refining strips out, so we pay more and we live with the variation.

And we leave the glycerin in. Saponification produces glycerin as a byproduct, and most commercial soapmakers pull it out and sell it, because it's worth more on its own and the bar lasts longer without it.
Ours stays. That's why the bar feels the way it does afterward, and it's also why it doesn't last as long. One decision, both consequences.
One fat. Four bars. The scent is a named essential oil on the back panel, or nothing at all.

bodies.name: Three weeks, or three months
lines: A customer told us the bar was a third gone after a week and eleven dollars was excessive. I want to take that seriously, because they were not wrong about the week.

Our bar dissolves faster than a tallow bar. That's the glycerin we left in, and glycerin pulls in water — which is exactly what you want against your skin and exactly what you don't want on a wet dish.
So the thing that decides how long this bar lasts isn't really the bar. It's drainage.
A coconut bar sitting in a puddle is gone in a fortnight. The same bar on something that drains lasts considerably longer. Same soap. Nothing changed but where you put it.
If you want the cost per bar down anyway, the four-pack works out at nine seventy-five and the twelve-pack at seven thirty-three.
I'm not going to tell you it's the cheapest soap you can buy. I'm telling you that almost everyone who told us it vanished was storing it in water.

bodies.name: Conditioned, not stripped
lines: If your skin reacts to things, you have probably never switched from body wash to a bar. You're right to be careful. Most bars earned that reputation honestly.
The squeak you get from a conventional bar is detergent lifting the oil off your skin. You were taught that squeak means clean. It means removed.
There's no detergent in ours. No sulfates. No rendered fat in the base. Saponified coconut oil and the glycerin that reaction made.
So it leaves a slightly grippy feel instead of a squeak, and some people genuinely don't like that. I'd rather you hear it from me.
Pure Unscented has no oils in it at all — not a masked scent, just nothing there — which is where I'd start if you react to things.

And one thing that's hard to find on any label, so I'll say it here: our Nourishing Tea Tree and our Refreshing Lemongrass both contain tea tree oil. If you avoid it, take the Calming Lavender or the Pure Unscented.

bodies.name: Soap, not detergent
lines: The pump by your kitchen sink probably isn't soap. That's not an insult — most of them are surfactant blends, and there's a real distinction underneath the word.
Look for cocamidopropyl betaine. Or SLS, or SLES. Those are detergents. They're cheap, they foam beautifully, and they are extremely good at their job.
Their job is lifting oil. All of it, including the oil your skin put there on purpose. That's the tight feeling thirty seconds later.
Ours is saponified organic virgin coconut oil — one ingredient in the base — diluted to the consistency a foaming pump needs.
It lifts oil and dirt without that stripping feel. Not because it's gentle in some vague way. Because it's different chemistry doing the lifting.
No SLS. No SLES. No cocamidopropyl betaine. No propylene glycol, no parabens, no triclosan, no EDTA, no dyes.
And every scent is a named essential oil on the back panel. There's no fragrance line hiding anything.

bodies.name: Hands in water all day
lines: We built this for hands that wash constantly. Nurses, chefs, bartenders, dishwashers, massage therapists, anyone with a newborn.
A customer put it better than we ever have — their hands are in water all day at work, and they said this locks moisture in better than anything they'd bought from the big bath chains.
Here's the boring reason. A detergent lifts every oil it meets, so thirty washes a shift is thirty strippings, and skin can't refill that fast.
There's no detergent in this bottle. It's saponified coconut oil, and the glycerin that reaction produces stays in rather than getting pulled out and sold.
So what you're managing after the tenth wash isn't dirt any more. It's what the first nine took off you.
One pump is enough. People tell us that constantly, which is why the eight-ounce goes further than eight ounces sounds like it should.

bodies.name: Why it's thin, and the refill
lines: Our hand soap is thinner than what you're used to. People tell us it feels watered down, so let me explain what thickness in a hand soap actually is.
In most commercial soap it's a thickener, added for one reason: you associate thick with concentrated. It does no cleaning whatsoever.
Ours is diluted to what a foaming pump needs, because the foamer does that work — it aerates a small amount into a full lather.
Which means one real warning. Put this in a standard pump and it comes out as a runny liquid and you'll think we sent you a bad batch. It has to be the foamer.
Thirteen dollars for the eight-ounce. Twenty-six for the thirty-two-ounce refill — four times the soap for twice the money.
We would rather sell you the refill. You buy the bottle once, and after that you're only buying soap, which is the only part you wanted.
